method: Curated research leads. Ordinal impact and feasibility are editorial judgments, not calibrated probabilities or measured risk reductions. Ranges express plausible disagreement. Evidence confidence concerns the mechanism, not predicted success. Coordination adds no automatic bonus.

routes.title: Turn compute procurement into an incident-response protocol
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment: timely security-incident evidence and mitigation could limit repeated or spreading compromise of shared AI infrastructure. Whether this reaches model-originated incidents needs interpretation; no model-release veto or quantified reduction in advanced-AI risk is established.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: an explicit notification duty and termination procedure are already written in the draft. Making a working protocol still needs final contract terms, contracting-authority action, contractor accommodation and clarity on tenant reporting. Those dependencies prevent an easy-to-implement rating.
routes.actor: EuroHPC Joint Undertaking and the relevant national contracting authorities; EU institutional participation is required, not just a coalition of national governments.
routes.obligor: The AIGF contractor. Direct obligations on model developers or tenants require examination of user terms and any applicable flow-down.
routes.instrument: Published model Framework Contract, I.14.6; security-breach termination ground II.18.1(p); procedure II.18.3. Draft text, not an executed agreement located in this review.
routes.safeguard: Clarify coverage of model-originated security incidents, then agree a notification, retained-evidence and mitigation protocol using the draft infrastructure-security duty as the starting point.
routes.verification: Contracting authorities receive breach notifications and continuing information. Proposed protocol would name required evidence, an accountable reviewer and an escalation process. Whether tenant inference evidence is available remains unresolved.
routes.remedy: Draft II.18.1(p) permits termination for specified security breaches, subject to II.18.3 notice and observations. An additional-measures request is not automatically an enforceable new duty.
routes.window: Published extension announcement: Lot 2 deadline 3 December 2026; Lot 1 deadline 4 February 2027. Older Lot 1 metadata still says 3 December. Confirm the current clarification cut-off before acting; later steps depend on signature and agreed terms.
routes.evidenceSummary: The retained model contract expressly links infrastructure-security notification and mitigation to a breach remedy and procedure. I.14.7 and Specific Contract 11.5 are request/reasonable-effort provisions, not unconditional powers to impose new model-safety terms.
routes.gap: No executed agreement or explicit model-harm reporting taxonomy was located. The scope of model-originated incidents and tenant obligations needs an authoritative interpretation.
routes.nextQuestion: Will the contracting authority confirm how I.14.6 applies to a model-mediated data breach on anchor-customer capacity, and which agreed user terms supply the reporting evidence?
incentives: Public purchasers gain visibility into security incidents affecting purchased compute.
Operators gain a common reporting protocol and clearer expectations rather than inconsistent requests.
constraints: Procurement amendments must not improperly change initial conditions or create unequal treatment.
The contractor must be able to obtain the relevant tenant evidence.
Reporting creates safety value only if findings prompt effective mitigation.

routes.title: Japan: safety-evidence requirements in national government AI procurement
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment, not measured risk reduction: evidence requirements could make evaluation, incident reporting and model-change notice conditions for covered government purchases. The platform's intended reach of approximately 180,000 officials indicates potential coverage, not purchasing power or vendor dependence. Wider adoption could spread the practice, but public-sector scope, domestic-model emphasis and the unknown baseline limit the claimed impact.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: one government's existing procurement platform and AISI-assisted governance standard give this proposal a comparatively direct administrative starting point. The rating is conditional on a lawful future tender or amendment. Current call terms, budget authority, vendor capacity, remedies and the AISI evaluation-to-policy operating mechanism were not established. Published rollout milestones are not evidence that procurement conditions remain open for negotiation.
routes.actor: Japan's Digital Agency (builds and operates the whole-of-government platform Gen-nai, runs its rolling foundation-model procurements, published the Gen-nai Standard); ministry CAIOs administer agency-side use; AISI Japan as technical evaluator.
routes.obligor: Vendors of foundation models and AI systems bidding into Gen-nai and successor government AI contracts — under current calls principally developers of domestically built Japanese models; the standard's required appropriate selection of domestic and foreign foundation models keeps foreign models in scope for platform eligibility.
routes.instrument: Proposed call specifications and contract conditions in Digital Agency AI procurements. The Gen-nai Standard is a documented government-side starting point, not an existing vendor covenant. The controlling procurement rules and whether amendments are permitted need review.
routes.safeguard: Vendor-side safety-evidence requirements as conditions of award and continued platform eligibility: pre-deployment safety-evaluation evidence or AISI testing access, incident reporting to government, and notice of material model changes. This extends the standard's existing government-side duties (foundation-model evaluation/selection system, high-risk determination sheet with CAIO reporting, human-in-the-loop, shadow-AI ban) across the contract line to the vendor. The safeguard is new: no fetched document imposes such duties on vendors.
routes.verification: Proposed: AISI-assisted evaluation evidence informs Digital Agency model selection and ministry risk determinations. AISI cooperation on the governance standard is documented. Assignment, capacity, evidence access and an operating vendor-evaluation process remain to be confirmed.
routes.remedy: Proposed: non-selection, suspension or termination where lawfully provided in the tender and signed contract, with notice and cure terms. Existing contract remedies were not reviewed; no AISI veto is established.
routes.window: Unknown procurement decision window. Published programme milestones include an agent-environment rollout targeted around December 2026 and wider use in FY2027. These do not establish an open tender, amendment right or available budget. Retrieve current call documents before treating this as an actionable opportunity.
routes.evidenceSummary: Four primary sources read 2026-10-31 document the machinery this route extends: (1) the Digital Agency operates Gen-nai for ~180,000 national officials with full-scale FY2027 rollout funded by ministry budgets, frames procurement and use of domestically developed AI as serving safe use and Japan's AI autonomy, and runs rolling calls (domestic-LLM call 2025-12-02, results 2026-03-06; pre-announcement 2026-05-29; domestic foundation models trialled on domestic cloud from 2026-07-10); (2) the Gen-nai Standard (2026-10-20), drafted with AISI, binds three government-side roles and requires a foundation-model evaluation/selection system and a risk-based approach under the AI Procurement and Utilization Guideline with a high-risk determination sheet and CAIO reporting; (3) the standard's governance diagram places the procurement guideline inside the AI Act-based framework covering policy through practice, and its quoted Basic Plan excerpt has the government lead proper procurement to raise the reliability and transparency of AI used across Japanese society; (4) the Second AI Basic Plan (2026-07-14) commits to AISI evaluation capabilities and to mechanisms translating evaluation results into policy, regulation and operations, with annual updates. No fetched document shows safety-evidence conditions in any call or any vendor duty in the standard — the safeguard is proposed, the mechanism documented.
routes.gap: Call documents for the 2025-12-02 call and the 2026-05-29 pre-announcement were not retrieved, so existing conditions and the next call's open/closed status are unknown; the AI Procurement and Utilization Guideline's own text, issuer, date and binding force were not located (referenced only inside the standard's overview); the AISI evaluation-to-policy mechanism has no located operating instrument; vendor capacity and willingness to supply evaluation evidence are unexamined; no quantified government AI spend was located to size the buyer lever.
routes.nextQuestion: Do the Gen-nai domestic-model call documents and the coming FY2027 full-scale-use tender contain safety-evaluation, incident-reporting or model-change conditions, and does the AI Procurement and Utilization Guideline bind vendors or only government users? Retrieving the call PDFs and the guideline text is the discriminating next step.
incentives: Vendors could gain access to a government platform intended for approximately 180,000 officials; spending and vendor dependence are not quantified.
The Digital Agency could connect its reliability and transparency goals to evidence requirements in future lawful procurements.
AISI Japan gains an operating channel for its evaluations, which the Second AI Basic Plan commits to wire into policy and operations.
The domestic-model preference gives Japanese LLM developers a commercial reason to accept evaluation conditions in exchange for stable government demand.
constraints: The Gen-nai Standard binds government users, ministry administrators and Digital Agency developers — not vendors; obligating vendors requires new call and contract text, so the safeguard's status is proposed.

Current calls target domestically developed models, so the immediate obligor set is Japanese model developers; foreign labs are reached only through the standard's domestic-and-foreign model-selection duty.

The route rests on the government's own contracting authority; Japan's AI Act imposes no lab obligations and no penalties (team-verified read of the Cabinet Office overview), and competitive-procurement and budget rules still apply.
AISI Japan has no veto, and its evaluation-to-policy translation mechanism is a Basic Plan commitment, not an operating pipeline.
Baseline unverified: existing call documents were not read, so the route cannot claim to add to conditions whose presence is unknown.

routes.title: Compatible AI procurement safety profile across Japan, Korea and Singapore
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment, not measured risk reduction: one shared evidence bar would gate three public-sector markets at once, and mutual recognition would give vendors a single evaluation covering Japanese-, Korean- and regional-language failure modes that English-centric testing under-serves, while removing each government's incentive to undercut the others' safety asks as they compete for AI-leadership positioning. Bounded above by genuine cross-acceptance of substantive AISI evaluations becoming a regional default; bounded below by a paperwork harmonization that adds formats without new testing or reach beyond government sales.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: joint AISI workshops and evaluation exercises offer a technical starting point. Governmental obstacles remain: this review did not locate mutual recognition of evaluation results for procurement, Singapore's whole-of-government procurement anchor, or authorization by the three governments for cross-acceptance. Different legal bases and multiple agencies add coordination costs. Technical cooperation does not establish procurement authority.
routes.actor: The three governments' AI-procurement and safety-institute authorities acting together: Japan's Digital Agency with AISI Japan; Korea's MSIT with its statutory AI Safety Institute (AI Basic Act Art. 12; the Public Procurement Service's role is unverified); Singapore's IMDA/GovTech with the Singapore AISI (Digital Trust Centre) — Singapore's whole-of-government AI procurement policy has not been located.
routes.obligor: Vendors of AI models and systems selling into the three governments' public-sector AI markets — foundation-model developers and integrators, and through them the labs whose models they deploy.
routes.instrument: Proposed common procurement clauses and an agreed evaluation-evidence recognition arrangement, adopted through each government's lawful procurement process. Technical guidance is a starting point, not contracting authority. Controlling procurement instruments in all three jurisdictions remain to be examined.
routes.safeguard: Proposed: a shared pre-deployment safety-evidence package covering Japanese-, Korean- and regional-language failure modes, accepted for covered purchases by all three governments, with compatible incident-reporting and model-change-notice clauses. No such recognition arrangement or common clause set was located in this review; absence from this evidence set does not establish absence across APAC.
routes.verification: Proposed: participating institutes evaluate against an agreed protocol, with procurement authorities accepting the results. Workshops and joint tests support technical feasibility, but neither evaluation equivalence nor procurement acceptance is established.
routes.remedy: Proposed: remedies expressly included in each jurisdiction's lawful tender and contract, potentially including non-selection or suspension. No common remedy, delisting power or executed clause set was located.
routes.window: No common procurement decision window was established. Published workshops and evaluation reports document cooperation, not government consent or open procurement negotiations. Retrieve current tenders and named decision-makers in each country.
routes.evidenceSummary: The reviewed primary sources document Japan-Korea AISI technical cooperation and Singapore's joint testing and evaluation activity. These provide a possible technical foundation for compatible evidence requirements, not an agreed purchasing arrangement. The shared procurement profile, recognition rules and government assent remain proposals. Korean statutory claims in the earlier working note were not re-verified against the amended controlling text and are not relied on here to establish procurement authority.
routes.gap: Singapore's whole-of-government AI procurement policy was not located. Korea's Public Procurement Service standards and amended AI Basic Act were not examined in this pass. Acceptance of foreign AISI evaluations for covered purchases is not established by these sources. Whether current tenders reference network evaluation formats is unknown. The operative procurement terms and government consent require direct verification.
routes.nextQuestion: Can the three institutes convert NAAIMES joint-testing methods into a shared evidence format that procurement officers accept — and does each government have a live procurement instrument to host it? First discriminating retrievals: Singapore's GovTech/IMDA procurement requirements, Korea's Public Procurement Service AI standards, and the Gen-nai call documents.
incentives: Vendors run one evaluation for three government markets instead of three duplicated ones, and gain a reason to test Japanese-, Korean- and regional-language failure modes that English-centric testing misses.
Governments could reduce duplicated testing and improve public-sector assurance if they agree on substantive evidence requirements.
A common evidence package could reduce vendor compliance work; savings and acceptance remain unmeasured.
The institutes gain uptake for methods they already co-produce — JAI-Trust, joint-testing formats, NAAIMES evaluator guidance.
Japan's planned AI Summit and Korea's APEC PPSTI chairmanship 2026-27 (team-verified) give each government a visible deliverable.
constraints: Mutual recognition for the proposed procurement route was not established by the sources reviewed.
Singapore's procurement-side anchor is missing: no whole-of-government AI procurement policy has been located in team research to date.

Three different legal bases — Korea's binding statute, Japan's guideline and contract machinery, Singapore's voluntary frameworks — must be bridged by a clause set rather than harmonized law, risking a lowest-common-denominator profile.
Multiple agencies per country must consent; there is no single contract hook comparable to Japan's Gen-nai platform.
Institute cooperation to date is technical and voluntary; nothing fetched shows any government has authorized cross-acceptance of evaluations for procurement.

routes.title: Use SG AISI agent data-leakage evaluations as a Singapore government deployment gate
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment, not a measured effect: a working gate would force remediation of the data-handling failures the SG-KR evaluation documents (runs that were fully correct yet 0% safe on safety criteria), but only for one country's deployments and only for bounded, non-adversarial leakage risk. Voluntary publication of test results does not by itself reduce risk; the effect depends on the gate actually blocking deployments, and it does not reach adversarial or frontier risks.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: existing evaluation capability and guidance recommending pre-deployment testing give a national gate a comparatively direct starting point. The rating assumes deploying agencies can lawfully adopt the proposed rule. Their authority and agreement, named-model reporting, thresholds, procurement compatibility and re-testing capacity still require confirmation; IMDA's coordination role alone does not establish control over every deployment.
routes.actor: IMDA, the overall government agency for the Singapore AISI (baseline policy and international AI-safety engagements), with the Digital Trust Centre running the technical testing; public-sector deploying agencies would be the gate's first users.
routes.obligor: Vendors and integrators whose AI agents are offered for Singapore government deployment. Extending the gate to private-sector deployments would need legal authority not located in these sources.
routes.instrument: No binding instrument located. Proposed: an administrative deployment rule or procurement condition making passage of a standardized agent data-leakage evaluation a precondition for deploying agents in defined government workflows. The existing layer is voluntary: IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (v1.5, May 2026) recommends pre-deployment agent testing, and IMDA's Starter Kit describes the testing process.
routes.safeguard: A deploy-time data-handling gate: before an agent runs in covered government workflows, it must pass realistic 12-task data-leakage evaluations with correctness and safety scored separately, and no/low-tolerance failure modes fixed and re-tested rather than averaged away.
routes.verification: SG AISI/DTC runs its existing open-source pipeline (built with KR AISI, published on the sgaisi GitHub) against the system as deployed - realistic MCP tool environments, task-specific LLM-judge rubrics plus sampled human validation - and records named pass/fail results against pre-set thresholds.
routes.remedy: Deployment deferred or denied until leakage failures are remediated and re-tested; post-deployment re-evaluation triggered by model or tool changes, following the framework's continuous-testing recommendation.
routes.window: Unknown. Evaluation capability and voluntary guidance are documented, but the reviewed sources fix no adoption or procurement decision date.
routes.evidenceSummary: The Singapore AISI (IMDA plus the NTU-hosted Digital Trust Centre) co-authored a June 2026 joint evaluation with the Korea AISI showing that none of three tested agents achieved fully correct and fully safe execution across 12 realistic tasks, and that high task completion does not imply safe data handling. IMDA's agentic-AI governance framework already recommends testing agents for safety and security before deployment, and IMDA, GovTech, CSA and Google have sandbox-tested computer-use agents for public-sector use cases. What is missing is the gate itself: no reviewed source makes evaluation results a condition of deployment.
routes.gap: No instruction, tender clause or service standard was located that conditions agent deployment on evaluation results. Current joint-testing practice anonymizes models, which a public gate could not rely on without change. The evaluations cover bounded, non-adversarial workflows, not prompt-injection or red-team attacks; in the January 2026 companion exercise human and LLM judges disagreed on about 18% of sampled safety judgements; and no settled standard exists for pass/fail thresholds.
routes.nextQuestion: Does any Singapore instruction, government tender or assurance-sandbox pilot already require AISI-style testing before an agent is deployed in government - and if so, are results tied to a pass/fail deployment decision or only advisory?
incentives: Government buyers gain deploy-time evidence on a documented failure mode instead of trusting vendor claims.
Vendors face one published testing bar with an open-source pipeline rather than bespoke agency demands.
IMDA's stated goal of trusted adoption is served by demonstrating agents can handle Singapore's data before deployment.
Gate results would create named-system evidence that the AISI network could reuse for shared practices.
constraints: Current evaluations anonymize models, which cannot support public pass/fail accountability without a practice change.
Leakage evaluations measure bounded, non-adversarial workflows; they do not cover adversarial attacks or frontier risks.
Judge-based scoring needs human validation and remains partly subjective; threshold-setting has no settled standard.
Binding deployments outside government would require legal authority not located in these sources.

routes.title: Singapore-Korea-Japan shared agent-evaluation evidence protocol feeding national deployment gates
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment, not a measured effect: evaluation evidence recognized across three significant AI markets would apply the same deploy-time data-handling pressure to more vendors and could seed the shared reporting standards the evaluation community says are missing. The measured failure mode remains operational data leakage in bounded workflows, not frontier or catastrophic risk; wider coverage is not observed risk reduction.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: the technical relationships exist through joint exercises, but this review did not establish the proposed binding protocol, shared thresholds, recognition arrangement or national deployment gates. The SG-KR report shows independent pipelines producing different scores on the same scenarios; recognition would need additional standardization and government agreement.
routes.actor: The three national AISIs - Singapore AISI (IMDA/Digital Trust Centre), Korea AISI and Japan AISI - working through the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (NAAIMES); each national government retains its own deployment authority.
routes.obligor: Agent vendors and integrators deploying across the three countries' public sectors; any obligation would arise through each country's own gate, not from the network, which has no legal mandate.
routes.instrument: No instrument located. Proposed: a protocol defining common agent data-leakage evaluation suites, a shared reporting format and agreed thresholds, and each country's acceptance of the others' evaluation evidence at its national deployment gate. Recognition is proposed, not established: the reviewed documents record voluntary technical cooperation only.
routes.safeguard: One recognized set of realistic agent data-leakage evaluations accepted by three national deployment gates, harmonizing no/low-tolerance failure modes so that a vendor which fixes leakage once satisfies three markets instead of negotiating three bespoke regimes.
routes.verification: Each institute runs the common open pipeline (the SG-KR agent-testing pipeline) in its own environment on the same scenarios, cross-validates samples with the other institutes, and publishes results in a shared format against agreed thresholds; each national gate then checks that evidence before deployment approval.
routes.remedy: Failure anywhere in the shared suite blocks or defers deployment at any participating gate until remediation and re-test; failure patterns would be disclosed to the vendor with re-testing evidence shared across the three.
routes.window: Unknown. The reviewed sources give no decision date for recognition or national deployment gates. Shared thresholds and recognition would require further agreement; a completion year cannot be inferred from the publication dates of technical guidance.
routes.evidenceSummary: The cooperation substrate is documented: institutes from Singapore, Japan and South Korea joined the third NAAIMES joint testing exercise on agentic safety (July 2025), whose sensitive-information-leakage and fraud strand Singapore led; the SG-KR bilateral exercise produced a shared 12-task leakage methodology, a joint June 2026 report and an open pipeline; a Singapore-Japan-UK-led multilingual exercise (February 2025) ran prompts across ten languages with Korean contributions and called for pre-standardized evaluation criteria; and NAAIMES' first best-practice document (July 2026) anticipates that governments will require high-quality evaluators. No reviewed document establishes shared thresholds, result recognition or deployment gates.
routes.gap: The reviewed evidence documents voluntary technical cooperation with anonymized models. This review did not locate an agreed evidence protocol, shared thresholds, mutual recognition or the proposed national deployment gates. The same scenarios scored differently in the SG and KR pipelines, so cross-acceptance would require further standardization. The network's February 2025 disclaimer states its tests do not establish that a system is safe or appropriate for release.
routes.nextQuestion: Is there any NAAIMES or ministerial commitment - trilateral or network-wide - to move from joint testing to officially shared or accepted evaluation results for deployment decisions, and does any of the three governments have a deployment gate that could accept such evidence?
incentives: Vendors avoid running similar leakage tests three times for three markets; one recognized evidence set lowers compliance cost.
Institutes already share pipelines and scenarios, so a protocol would formalize existing practice rather than start from zero.
Three markets jointly exert more vendor pull than Singapore alone, raising the cost of shipping leaky agents into the region.
Harmonized thresholds could lift the regional floor and seed the shared reporting standards the evaluation community says are missing.
constraints: Each of the three governments must first adopt a national deployment gate; the protocol multiplies the national route's missing step by three.
The same scenarios produced materially different scores in the SG and KR pipelines; reproducibility limits how far results can be recognized without heavy standardization.
Anonymized-model practice conflicts with the named evidence a gate needs; current exercises publish methodology, not verdicts.
NAAIMES has no legal mandate; recognition would rest on separate administrative acts across three different legal systems.
The network's own first best-practice document (July 2026) explicitly excludes agentic evaluations from its scope.

sources.title: SG AISI and KR AISI, An Evaluation of Data Leakage Risks in Tool-Using LLM Agents in Realistic Scenarios

routes.title: Canada attaches a model-safety covenant to future stages of its announced equity investment in Cohere
routes.impactRationale: Editor judgment, not a measured effect. If implemented, the covenant binds one named frontier-adjacent company group (Cohere, whose announced merger with Aleph Alpha spans Canada and Germany) with up to roughly $1.6 billion of staged public money behind it. That is a concrete obligor, but one company in one investment, with no release-control power, an unknown remedy and an existing voluntary CAISI cooperation undertaking that shrinks the marginal safety addition. The upside is a replicable sovereign-investment template for other middle powers; the downside is reporting-only terms with no operational content.
routes.feasibilityRationale: A single government designing terms for its own staged equity needs no coalition, and the announcement itself supplies the attachment points: staged funding, a regular-reporting architecture and an existing CAISI cooperation undertaking. What holds feasibility at mid-scale is the missing instrument: no vehicle, subscription agreement, tranche architecture or draw condition is on the record, so whether any future stage is actually conditional (rather than precommitted or unconditional) is unknown, and any covenant needs Cohere's written assent.
routes.actor: Government of Canada (announced by the Prime Minister; the investing legal vehicle is unnamed - CDEV is not established as the holder)
routes.obligor: Cohere (Toronto-founded; the release also describes a recent merger with Germany's Aleph Alpha, so the obligor group spans two jurisdictions)
routes.instrument: Announced staged equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Cohere (29 October 2026, alongside private investors including NVIDIA, Bell and Schwarz Group; co-investor amounts unstated). The release says only '$', so CAD is inferred, not stated. No subscription or shareholders agreement has been located; 'made in stages' with 'regular reporting' is the only documented structure.
routes.safeguard: Proposed: a model-safety covenant attached to future equity stages - for example defined safety-milestone or incident-reporting deliverables to the government or the Canadian AI Safety Institute (formalizing the company's announced undertaking to keep working with CAISI), an evaluation-access right, and an evidence standard with a stated consequence for non-delivery.
routes.verification: The release announces 'regular reporting on progress against the company's commitments, including jobs and investment in Canada' - with no recipient, cadence, evidence standard or safety deliverable. The reporting sentence is non-exhaustive ('including'), so a verification design (e.g. CAISI-delivered evaluation reports) is part of the proposal, not the record.
routes.remedy: None stated. 'Hold the company accountable' is announced reporting language, not an enumerated remedy, cure period or draw-stop. Withholding a later tranche would require the unlocated instrument to make future draws conditional; present discretion over later stages is unknown, not assumed.
routes.window: No tranche schedule, decision dates or stage architecture appear in the release. The investment was announced 2026-10-29 and may be in implementation now, but whether any future-stage terms remain negotiable - or are already fixed - is unknown. Recorded as unknown, not open.
routes.evidenceSummary: The retained, hashed PM release (read in full this session; SHA-256 and byte size re-verified against data/finance-research/sources.json) documents: an equity investment 'up to $1.6 billion', 'made in stages', with 'regular reporting' and 'hold the company accountable' language; five company undertakings, including to 'keep working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute to champion the safe development and use of advanced AI' and to commit at least $1.7 billion to additional computing infrastructure in Canada by 2030; and the Aleph Alpha merger. String searches on the operative text confirm zero occurrences of 'CDEV', 'Development Investment', 'veto', 'board', 'consent' and 'CAD' (the only raw-HTML hits for 'board'/'consent' are page chrome: 'modal_keyboard', 'gtag consentMode'). The retained CDEV Act documents a plausible vehicle's statutory capacity (s.11(b) investing in shares or securities; s.21 investee-information privilege) but never mentions Cohere.
routes.gap: No executed investment instrument was located in this review. Investing vehicle, signatory, tranche architecture, draw conditions, governance or information rights, explicit currency unit and safety deliverables remain unknown. CDEV is not established as the investor; the announced stages may be unconditional, conditional or precommitted. The CAISI cooperation undertaking has no located operating terms.
routes.nextQuestion: Which legal vehicle holds the staged investment, and what conditions govern later-stage draws - unconditional staged calls, conditional tranches with certifications, or precommitted subscriptions? Locate the subscription/shareholders agreement or a ministerial statement naming the vehicle and tranche conditions.
incentives: Sovereign-AI framing: the release justifies the investment as securing Canadian AI sovereignty, giving the government a stated interest in defined deliverables for public money.
The announcement already contains an accountability architecture - staged funding plus regular reporting - that a safety covenant could specify rather than invent.
Cohere's announced undertaking to keep working with CAISI provides a safety counterpart and a hook the covenant could formalize with deliverables and standards.
A worked sovereign-equity covenant would be a replicable template for other middle powers negotiating AI investments.
constraints: No located instrument: the covenant requires Cohere's written assent - equity cannot impose operational terms unilaterally - and the vehicle, signatory and tranche terms are unknown.

The release contains no veto, board, consent or governance right (string-verified zero hits in the operative text) and no remedy, cure period or draw-stop; 'hold the company accountable' is reporting language.
CDEV is not established as the investor; if another vehicle or a new fund invests, the CDEV Act analysis does not apply and that vehicle's statute and appropriation constraints govern instead.
Terms may already be fixed: 'made in stages' does not establish that later stages are discretionary; present discretion is unknown and must not be assumed either way.
Currency is unstated ('$' only): any CAD figure must be flagged as inferred. The post-merger group structure (Aleph Alpha) complicates which entity bears covenants and under which law.

routes.title: Taiwan attaches model-safety conditions to access to publicly supported AI compute under the AI Basic Law
routes.impactRationale: Editor judgment, not a measured effect. Conditions on Taiwan's public compute bind only that compute's users, whose identity, scale and frontier relevance are unknown, so direct impact on frontier-model safety is plausibly small. The upside runs through Article 16's internationally interoperable risk taxonomy (definitions other jurisdictions could adopt) and the route's value as a replicable national template. No reach to global frontier developers is evidenced, and this route claims no semiconductor leverage.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: a national support programme could be a relatively direct route if an authorized administrator can set future access conditions. But no applicable programme, budget, access policy or user base was established here. Recipient agreements, budget rules and existing commitments may constrain changes. The Act's implementation timetable does not establish a compute-programme negotiation window.
routes.actor: Government of Taiwan (the National Science and Technology Council is the central competent authority under Article 2; the Ministry of Digital Affairs leads the risk taxonomy under Article 16; the Executive Yuan convenes the National AI Strategic Committee under Article 6)
routes.obligor: Recipients and users of Taiwan's public AI compute and support measures - none identified in this evidence set
routes.instrument: Proposed: conditions attached to access to publicly supported AI compute (subsidies, funding, infrastructure and support measures of the kind Article 10 authorizes and Article 11 mandates for emerging-AI development and testing). The Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (promulgated 2026-01-14) is the enabling statute; it contains no compute-program terms and none may be inferred.
routes.safeguard: Proposed: safety conditions on public-compute access - for example pre-release testing records, model-incident reporting, or disclosure against the Article 16 interoperable AI risk taxonomy, with Article 5-style advisory machinery and MODA assessment/verification tools as candidate verification infrastructure.
routes.verification: Not established on the record. Article 10 requires an annual performance-report system with regular public announcement of results and evaluation opinions for AI support policies, and Articles 5 and 16 point to MODA-provided assessment/verification tools and an interoperable taxonomy that could define evidence - but no compute-program verification mechanism exists in the evidence.
routes.remedy: Not established: the Basic Law contains no program-level draw-stop, cure period or enforcement mechanism. Article 16(3) requires the circumstances listed in Article 5(1) to be restricted or prohibited 'in accordance with the law' - a duty on future risk-based regulation, not a program remedy. Any remedy would be designed into future program terms.
routes.window: Dated legislative hooks, unknown program calendar. The Act took effect on promulgation, 2026-01-14 (Article 20), and Article 18 requires non-complying laws, regulations and administrative measures to be enacted, amended or repealed within two years of the effective date - by 2028-01-14. That is a documented window for implementing acts; whether any public-compute program decision falls inside it is unknown.
routes.evidenceSummary: The official English text of Taiwan's Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (NSTC laws system; promulgated 2026-01-14, effective the same day per Article 20) was fetched and read in full this session. Article 10 has the government handle subsidies, commissions, funding, investments, incentives and fiscal measures for AI, with an annual public performance-report system; Article 16 has the Ministry of Digital Affairs promote an AI risk taxonomy interoperable with international frameworks and assist industry competent authorities with risk-based management regulations, with Article 16(3) requiring Article 5(1) circumstances to be restricted or prohibited by law; Article 19 requires government agencies using AI in duties or services to conduct risk assessments and plan response measures; Articles 2, 5, 6, 11, 18 and 20 supply the competent-authority assignment, high-risk advisory machinery, National AI Strategic Committee, development/testing support measures, the two-year implementing window and the effective date. No article specifies compute-program grant terms or access conditions.
routes.gap: No public-compute program document exists in this evidence set: whether Taiwan operates subsidized AI compute, at what scale, for whom, under what access terms and budget, is unknown. The Basic Law's articles are enabling and duty provisions - specific grant terms are not inferred from them. Which agency will run any compute program, and what the framework provisions mean in practice, depend on implementing acts not yet located. confidence is Low for this reason: the law is promulgated and primary-read, but the route's operative instrument is absent from the record, not merely unstudied.
routes.nextQuestion: Which Taiwanese program actually allocates public AI compute, at what scale and to whom, and on what published access terms - and does the Article 18 two-year window (to 2028-01-14) include any compute-support or subsidy regulation now in draft? Obtain program guidelines or budget lines to see whether safety conditions could attach.
incentives: A freshly promulgated Basic Law with a dated two-year implementing window (Article 18, to 2028-01-14) creates institutional momentum and a deadline for designing support-program rules now.
A national programme could offer a direct policy channel if its administrator has authority and applicable agreements permit the proposed conditions.
Article 16's interoperable-risk-taxonomy mandate supplies ready-made definitions any compute-access condition could reference, easing international legibility.
Article 10's annual public performance-report system creates a standing transparency mechanism that could carry safety-condition reporting.
constraints: Specific grant terms may not be inferred from the Basic Law: Articles 10, 16 and 19 are enabling and duty provisions, and no compute-program access condition exists on the record.

No assumed chip control: nothing in this route rests on Taiwan controlling TSMC, chip exports or any corporate chip supply; the leverage is public compute access only, and no program document evidences its scale or users.
Public AI compute programs are unevidenced here: existence, budget, users and substitutability are unknown, and no evidence suggests frontier labs depend on Taiwanese public compute.
Framework-law limits: the Basic Law operates through later regulations and program design (Article 18 window to 2028-01-14), so its practical force depends on implementing acts not yet made.
Article 19's risk assessments bind the government's own use of AI, not private developers; extending conditions to external compute users is design work, not existing law.

routes.title: Multinational lenders negotiate a model-safety covenant into new Anthropic credit (incremental facilities, extensions, refinancings or agreed amendments)
routes.impactRationale: Editor judgment, not a measured effect. A negotiated covenant would reach a frontier developer through enforceable credit-documentation machinery and could set a precedent that standardizes safety reporting across AI-lab lending - the strongest direct-reach candidate of this set. But the scope would be whatever the parties agree (possibly reporting-only), it can attach only to new paper with no holdback of committed draws, and the marginal safety gain over whatever Anthropic already does voluntarily (not evidenced here) is unknown.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: the filed credit-agreement text documents negotiating gates, but a covenant needs borrower initiation or agreement. Lender holdings are redacted, so voting arithmetic cannot be established; alternative lenders may substitute for unwilling new-money providers. No live negotiation or supportive coalition was identified. The broader-agreement colour reflects the need for commercial parties including the US borrower, not a claim that every lender must agree.
routes.actor: Lenders party to Anthropic's amended and restated credit agreement (multinational syndicate; roster and allocations unknown - Schedule 2.01 is redacted and the named arrangers are not confirmed lenders, so no nationality tally is asserted)
routes.obligor: Anthropic PBC (Borrower), with the Loan Parties and Guarantors reached through the Material Intellectual Property perimeter (s.5.12)
routes.instrument: Amended and Restated Credit Agreement dated as of September 4, 2026 (Exhibit 10.10 to Anthropic's Form S-1; New York law per s.9.15). Documented gates: any Lender's election to provide incremental commitments (s.2.21), to extend its loans/commitments (s.2.22) or to provide Replacement Revolving Facility Commitments (s.2.23: 'may elect or decline, in its sole discretion') is in that Lender's sole discretion; amendments otherwise require a writing entered into by the Borrower and the Required Lenders - Lenders holding more than 50% of outstanding Incremental Term Loans and Revolving Facility Commitments (s.1.01, s.9.08(b)) - with each directly adversely affected Lender's consent for enumerated matters (s.9.08(b)(i)).
routes.safeguard: Proposed: a model-safety covenant - e.g. safety-incident reporting to the Administrative Agent, evaluation-evidence delivery, or notification duties - negotiated into new incremental credit, an extension, a refinancing amendment, or an agreed s.9.08 amendment. Never a holdback of compliant committed draws, which the agreement does not permit.
routes.verification: A proposed covenant would ride existing reporting-covenant mechanics; s.5.05(b)'s covered-foreign-person notice to the Administrative Agent is an adjacent, documented information covenant. No safety covenant or verification standard exists in the reviewed text: a literal keyword scan of the retained text found no safety-labeled provision, and a clause-by-clause policy review was not performed, so indirect reach is unproven, not disproven.
routes.remedy: Ex ante only: refusing to elect new money or withholding amendment consent. No remedial power over existing compliant loans is claimed. The general covenant-default machinery (events of default, acceleration) was not extracted in this task - recorded as missing, not asserted absent. s.9.08(b)(i) protects each directly adversely affected Lender on enumerated economic fundamentals.
routes.window: Unknown: the s.2.21/s.2.22/s.2.23 gates open only on Borrower-initiated new credit, and s.9.08 amendments need the Borrower plus Required Lenders. The retained text dates no such event - the Closing Date, 2026-09-04, is the only relevant documented date - so whether any window is open at any given time, including now, is unknown.
routes.evidenceSummary: The retained tool-extracted text of the filed exhibit (682,490 characters; the direct raw fetch returned HTTP 403 and was not re-downloaded per coordinator instruction; SHA-256 and byte size re-verified against data/finance-research/sources.json this session) documents: 'AMENDED AND RESTATED CREDIT AGREEMENT dated as of September 4, 2026, among ANTHROPIC, PBC, as the Borrower'; sole-discretion lender elections in s.2.21 and s.2.22 ('any election to do so shall be in the sole discretion of such Lender') and s.2.23 ('may elect or decline, in its sole discretion'); the s.9.08(b) amendment gate ('pursuant to an agreement or agreements in writing entered into by the Borrower and the Required Lenders'); the Required Lenders definition (>50%); 'SCHEDULE 2.01Commitments[***]' and '[Signature Pages Intentionally Omitted]'. Named arrangers span several jurisdictions, but arranger titles do not establish lender status. confidence is Medium: the gates are documented in signed-instrument text, but at reduced provenance grade with a redacted roster.
routes.gap: Lender roster and allocations are redacted, so consent arithmetic is impossible; the facility amount is absent from the retained text; window openness is unknown; whether any lender, government or coalition has appetite for safety terms is wholly unevidenced; and the evidence is retained tool text at reduced provenance grade (raw bytes not retained; the S-1 body was not read).
routes.nextQuestion: Who actually holds the commitments (obtain Schedule 2.01 or an authoritative allocation disclosure), and is any Borrower-initiated incremental, extension or refinancing event live or foreseeable? Without both, consent arithmetic and window claims stay unknowable.
incentives: Every new-money election is already in each lender's sole discretion, so a safety-motivated lender can condition its own participation without any statute or charter change.
The documented amendment machinery (Borrower plus Required Lenders) supplies a lawful, ordinary route to add a covenant.
A negotiated precedent in one frontier lab's facility could standardize safety reporting across AI credit markets as other labs syndicate.
Banks' risk-management incentives could favor information covenants if they believe model-safety incidents threaten borrower value or collateral.
constraints: Borrower agreement is essential: gates are Borrower-initiated (ss.2.21-2.23) or require the Borrower plus Required Lenders (s.9.08(b)); nothing lets lenders impose terms on an already compliant committed draw.

Consent arithmetic is impossible: Schedule 2.01 is redacted and signature pages omitted, so who constitutes the Required Lenders (>50%) is unknown; named arrangers are not confirmed lenders and no nationality tally is asserted.
Each lender elects individually at sole discretion; a safety-motivated minority cannot block a facility that other lenders fund.
Window unknown: no Borrower-initiated new-credit event is dated or evidenced as live; the leverage is prospective negotiating position, not demonstrated bargaining strength.

No middle-power government actor is evidenced: the route runs through commercial banks whose incentives and any policy influence are speculation here; Anthropic's financing alternatives are unpriced and must never be treated as cheap substitutes.
